text:
Free the Curb: Why Cities Should Scrap Minimum Parking Requirements

Walk through almost any American city and you will find an enormous amount of land doing very little. Asphalt stretches behind supermarkets, around apartment blocks and in front of small restaurants, empty for most of the year. This is not an accident. It is the result of rules that tell builders exactly how many parking spaces they must supply, whether or not anyone wants them. Cities should abolish these minimum parking requirements, and the sooner the better.

Start with the basic problem. A parking mandate is a decision made by a planner about what a private business or home builder needs. Nobody knows better than a restaurant owner how many customers arrive by car. Nobody knows better than a housing developer how many future tenants will own one. Yet the standard rules ignore local knowledge and apply formulas, often drawn from a handbook of suburban traffic counts, to every site in town. The formulas are frequently wrong. Studies of apartment buildings and shopping centers regularly find lots that never fill, even at the busiest hour of the year. The rule demands a surplus and then locks it in forever.

That surplus is expensive. A single surface space can cost thousands of dollars to build, and a space in an underground garage can cost tens of thousands. Those costs do not vanish. They are passed to tenants as higher rents, to shoppers as higher prices and to homebuyers as higher purchase prices. Worse, they are charged to everyone equally. A household without a car still pays for the parking it is forced to buy. Requirements therefore work as a quiet tax on the poor, the young and the elderly, who are the people least likely to drive.

The mandates also strangle housing at a time when most cities are desperate for more of it. A small lot cannot hold a modest apartment building if half the site must be given over to cars. Many promising projects never get built because the parking math will not work. Others get built with fewer homes than the land could support. Where a developer might have fit twenty apartments, the rules allow twelve. Every missing home is a family priced out, or pushed to a distant suburb with a long commute. If we are serious about affordability, removing a rule that forces us to build car storage instead of homes is one of the cheapest reforms available.

Then there is the question of what our cities look like. Mandatory parking spreads buildings apart. Shops sit behind lots and homes sit behind driveways. Walking becomes unpleasant and sometimes impossible, so people drive even for short trips, which then creates a fresh excuse for more parking. It is a loop that feeds itself. Older neighborhoods built before these rules, such as historic main streets and compact downtowns, are often the places residents love most and the ones that generate the most tax revenue per acre. Many of them would be illegal to build today.

Critics raise a fair worry. If a new building has no parking, will its residents simply clog the neighborhood streets? The answer is that removing a requirement is not the same as banning parking. Developers will still build it wherever customers want it, because a building without parking where parking is needed will struggle to rent. What changes is the quantity becomes a market choice. In places that have already reformed, such as Buffalo, Minneapolis and Auckland, builders did not abandon parking altogether. They built less of it, tailored it to the site, and in some cases unbundled it so that tenants pay only for the space they use. Meanwhile the cities that dropped mandates saw the freed land turned into housing, shops and public space.

Street congestion is a real issue, but it has a better remedy than forcing everyone to build more lots. Cities can price curb parking sensibly, with meters that rise when a street is busy and residential permits where spillover is a concern. Revenue from that pricing can be returned to the neighborhood for sidewalks and trees. This approach treats parking as the scarce public resource it is, rather than pretending it is free and then wondering why it is always full.

Some will say that transit is too weak in their city to function without cars, so mandates are a necessity. But this confuses cause and effect. Car dependence is partly a product of the rules, and relaxing them does not force anyone out of their vehicle. A resident who loves driving can still drive. The reform simply stops forcing those who do not into subsidizing those who do.

The case for change is also about humility. Planners cannot predict how a neighborhood will want to live in twenty years. Cars may be shared, driven by software or replaced by something else entirely. A rule written in stone today will leave a legacy of unused concrete tomorrow. Flexibility is the safer bet.

None of this requires cities to be radical. They can phase the change in, starting with downtowns, transit corridors and small businesses, and then extend it citywide once the results are clear. Several cities have done exactly that without disaster.

The principle is simple. People and builders should decide how much parking they need, and the public should not be made to pay for the rest. Scrap the mandates and let our cities make room for homes, businesses and people again.
